## Basis
This report presents the design of a spray dryer and sets out the basis on which the design has been carried out. The design throughput of the dryer is 34 t per day. The duty that the dryer is required to perform is the removal of 97% of the key component from the feed. In other words, the feed comes in as a liquid in which the key component is present, and the product is required to leave as a dry powder from which the great majority of that component has been removed.

The feed itself is a pumpable liquid. It is atomised at the top of the drying chamber, so that it enters the hot air as a spray of fine droplets, and the droplets are dried as they travel through the chamber. The dried powder is collected partly from the chamber itself and partly from the separation stage that is fitted on the exhaust air leaving the chamber. It is important to appreciate that everything else in this report — the sizing of the equipment, the selection of materials, and the discussion of risks — is built on the basis described in this section: a stated throughput, a stated removal duty, a liquid feed going in, and a powder product coming out. If any of those things were different, the design would be different too.

As far as materials are concerned, all wetted parts of the dryer are to be made in 316L stainless steel. This statement is made here, in the basis, and it is not repeated elsewhere in the report; the materials section develops what follows from it.

Finally, the scope of the design should be understood. The design covers the dryer itself together with its own auxiliaries. What happens before the dryer — the preparation of the feed — and what happens after it — the handling of the powder — are outside the scope of this design.

It is also worth emphasising what kind of duty this is. Taking out nearly all of a component is considerably more demanding than taking out most of it, even at the same throughput, because the last part of the removal is where the air, the heat and the chamber volume are spent.

## Sizing
The sizing of the dryer is based on the throughput given in the basis, namely the 34 t per day of feed, together with the removal duty that the basis lays down. This section explains, in general terms, how the principal parts of the machine have been sized, proceeding from the atomiser outwards.

The atomiser that has been selected is a rotary atomiser. This choice has been made because the feed is a liquid from which a fine and even powder is required, and because a rotary atomiser is relatively tolerant of variations in the condition of the feed, which a pressure nozzle would tend to pass on to the spray. The rotating wheel breaks the feed up into droplets at the top end of the chamber, and in a very real sense everything that comes after the wheel is sized by reference to the droplets that it produces. The size of the droplets determines how long each droplet needs to spend in the hot air, and that drying time in turn determines the size of the chamber.

The chamber has accordingly been sized with two considerations in mind: the time that the droplets need in order to dry, and the path that the air takes as it passes through the chamber. The air comes in hot and meets the spray, giving up its heat in order to carry out the evaporation that the duty requires. The volume of the chamber is such as to hold the droplets in the air for the necessary length of time, while the shape of the chamber is intended to keep the wettest of the droplets away from the walls for as much of that time as the geometry will permit.

The air system — the heater, the fan and the separation stage — has been sized on the evaporation that has to be achieved. The heater must raise the whole of the air flow to the inlet condition, the fan must move that air through the chamber and through the separation stage, and the separation stage, which consists of cyclones with a polishing step on the exhaust, must recover the fine powder that the air carries out of the chamber. The exhaust air leaves the system carrying the removed component with it, and the separation stage is there to make sure that, as far as is reasonably possible, what leaves is vapour rather than product.

## Materials
All of the wetted parts of the dryer are made in the stainless steel grade that is stated in the basis section. By wetted parts is meant every surface that can come into contact with the feed, with the powder, with the wash liquor that is used to clean the machine, or with condensate from the exhaust. This includes the chamber and its roof, the atomiser and the pipe that feeds it, the ducting, the separation stage, and the outlets through which the powder leaves the machine.

The reason for the choice of grade is the range of contact that the wetted surfaces have to withstand. The feed is a liquid, and it will inevitably remain in the machine whenever the machine is stopped. The powder is the product, and its quality is affected by the surfaces it passes over. And the machine is washed down between campaigns, so that over the course of its life the wetted surfaces are exposed in turn to the product, the feed, the cleaning liquor and the air. The grade stated in the basis is able to resist this whole range of contact without relying on a coating that might fail or a lining that might lift, and it can be cleaned to a standard that the product requires.

Parts of the machine that do not come into contact with the process — the supporting steelwork, the cladding, the casing of the heater and the casing of the fan — are made of carbon steel with a protective coating, since what they have to withstand is weather and mechanical load rather than chemical contact. The dividing line between the two materials follows the wetted boundary throughout the machine, and any part that is wetted on one side, even if it is structural on the other, is treated as a wetted part.

Seals, gaskets and flexible connections have been selected to suit the same duties as the parts they connect, including the temperatures found in the air path. Joints in the powder path have been made flush and capable of being cleaned, and access has been provided so that the wetted surfaces can be inspected without the machine having to be dismantled.

## Risks
There are two significant risks that remain open at the conclusion of this design, and this section describes them honestly rather than attempting to design them away. They are fouling and turndown, and neither of them has been resolved by the work reported here.

Fouling means the gradual build-up of product in places where the product ought simply to pass through. In a spray dryer, the vulnerable places are well known. Deposits can form at the atomiser, where even a small build-up can throw the wheel out of balance and make the spray coarser. They can form on the walls of the chamber, where a layer of material insulates the wall, can scorch, and can eventually fall away into the product. And they can form in the separation stage, where the passages become progressively narrower. The design does what it can to reduce the exposure — the shape of the chamber is intended to keep the wettest spray away from the walls, and the access provided allows deposits to be found and cleaned off — but it would be misleading to describe this as a solution. This risk will only be closed when the machine has been run on the feed and the rate of fouling has been observed for real.

Turndown is the risk at the opposite end of the operating range. The dryer has been designed for its stated throughput, but a plant does not always call for the full rate. At reduced rates, the atomiser produces a different spray, the balance between the air and the feed changes, and the margins that the design relies on to keep wet powder away from the walls and out of the exhaust are used up in a different pattern. The lowest throughput at which the dryer will still perform its duty satisfactorily has not been established, and no figure for it is given in this report. The risk will be closed when turndown has either been tested or guaranteed on the basis of evidence; in the meantime, anyone operating the dryer below its design rate should be aware that they are operating outside the scope of what this report covers.

The sizing stands for the duty laid down in the basis. The risks stand alongside it, unresolved.
target:
## Basis
The design covers a spray dryer with a design throughput of 34 t per day. The duty of the dryer is the removal of 97% of the key component from the feed: the feed enters as a liquid carrying the key component, and the product leaves as a dry powder from which all but the remainder of that component has been taken.

The feed is a pumpable liquid. It is atomised at the top of the drying chamber, and the droplets dry in the hot air that shares the chamber with them. The powder is collected from the chamber and from the separation stage on the exhaust air. What the dryer is asked to do is fixed by the two figures above and by the form of the feed and the product: a stated rate, a stated removal, a liquid in and a powder out. The sizing, the materials and the risks in this report all hang on that statement, and nothing outside it is designed here.

Materials are 316L stainless steel for all wetted parts. The grade is stated here, once, and the materials section works from this statement without repeating it.

The boundary of the design is the dryer and its own auxiliaries. Feed preparation upstream of the dryer and powder handling downstream of it are outside the boundary. The design takes the feed as it is delivered to the dryer, and it delivers powder and exhaust air across the boundary in the other direction. Conditions at the interfaces are the conditions of the plant the dryer serves, and they are inputs to this design, not outputs of it.

The duty is a removal duty, and what that means for the rest of the design is stated plainly. A dryer asked to take out nearly all of a component is a different machine from one asked to take out most of it, even at the same throughput: the last of the removal is the expensive part, in air, in heat and in chamber, and the sizing that follows is a sizing for the stated removal, not for a lesser one that would be easier to reach.

## Sizing
The dryer is sized on the throughput of the basis, the 34 t per day of feed, and on the removal the basis states. Sizing proceeds from the atomiser outward.

The atomiser is a rotary atomiser, chosen because the feed is a liquid whose duty is a fine, even powder, and because the rotary form tolerates the variation in feed state that a pressure nozzle passes on to the spray. The wheel throws the feed into droplets at the top of the chamber, and everything downstream of the wheel is sized on the droplets it makes: their size sets the time each droplet needs in the air, and that time sets the chamber.

The chamber is sized on drying time and on the path the air takes through it. The air enters hot, meets the spray, and gives up its heat to the evaporation the duty requires; the chamber volume holds the droplets in the air for the time the drying takes, and the chamber shape keeps the wettest droplets off the walls for as much of that time as the geometry allows. The diameter is set by the air path and the spray pattern together, and the height by the fall the droplets need. Neither figure is a catalogue figure; both follow from the throughput and the removal, and both would change if either changed.

The air system is sized on the evaporation. The heater raises the full air flow to the inlet condition, the fan moves it through the chamber and the separation stage, and the separation stage, cyclones with a polishing step on the exhaust, returns the fines the air carries out of the chamber. The exhaust leaves with the removed component in it, and the separation stage is sized so that what leaves in the exhaust is vapour and as little powder as the stage can hold back.

## Materials
All wetted parts are built in the stainless steel grade stated in the basis. Wetted parts are every surface the feed, the powder, the wash liquor or the exhaust condensate can touch: the chamber and its roof, the atomiser and its feed pipe, the ducts, the separation stage, and the powder outlets.

The grade is chosen for the contact it has to survive. The feed is a liquid that will sit in the machine during every stoppage, the powder is the product and takes its standing from the surfaces it touches, and the machine is washed down between campaigns, so the wetted surfaces meet the product, the feed, the wash and the air in turn. The grade named in the basis resists that range of contact without a coating to fail or a lining to lift, and it can be cleaned to a standard the product can accept.

Structure that does not meet the process, the supporting steelwork, the cladding, the heater casing, the fan casing, is carbon steel, protected by coating, because its duty is weather and load rather than contact. The division between the two materials follows the wetted boundary everywhere, and where a part is wetted on one face and structural on the other, it is built as a wetted part.

Seals, gaskets and flexible connections are picked for the same contact as the parts they join, and for the temperatures of the air path they sit in. Joints in the powder path are made flush and cleanable, and the chamber is fitted with access that lets the wetted surfaces be inspected without dismantling the machine. A material that cannot be inspected cannot be kept, and inspection is part of the materials decision, not an afterthought to it.

## Risks
Two risks stand open at the end of this design: fouling, and turndown. Neither is resolved here, and this section states them as open items, with the condition on which each would close.

Fouling is the risk that the product builds up where it should pass through. A spray dryer fouls at the places where wet or sticky powder meets a surface: at the atomiser, where a deposit unbalances the wheel and coarsens the spray; on the chamber walls, where a layer insulates, scorches and falls into the product; and in the separation stage, where the passages narrow. The design reduces the exposure, in that the chamber shape keeps the wettest spray off the walls and the access the materials section provides lets deposits be found and removed, but reduction is not resolution. How fast this feed fouls this machine, and how often it must be cleaned, are questions the design cannot answer, because they rest on the behaviour of the actual feed over actual campaigns. The risk closes when the machine has run the feed and the fouling rate has been seen; until then it stands.

Turndown is the risk at the other end of the rate. The dryer is designed at its stated throughput, and a plant does not always ask for the full rate. Below it, the atomiser makes a different spray, the air-to-feed balance shifts, and the margin the design carries against wet powder reaching the wall or the exhaust is spent differently. The lowest rate at which the dryer still makes its duty has not been established, and the design does not state one. The risk closes when the turndown has been tested or guaranteed on evidence; until then, operation below the design rate is operation outside what this report covers.

Both risks are stated here rather than designed away, because a design report that hides its open items behind its sizing is worse than one that names them. The sizing stands for the duty of the basis. The risks stand beside it, open.
